Iterative self-distillation — where a model is repeatedly trained on its own outputs with confidence sharpening (e.g., temperature annealing or label smoothing removal) — creates a feedback loop in which the student's attention distributions progressively concentrate on a shrinking set of tokens, a phenomenon measurable as monotonically decreasing attention entropy across distillation rounds. The central question is whether this entropy collapse is a feature (cleaner, more decisive routing) or a pathology (loss of coverage over semantically relevant context), and the answer depends critically on which heads collapse: task-relevant heads sharpening is fine; heads responsible for broad coreference or long-range dependency coverage collapsing is catastrophic and silent in aggregate metrics. In ensemble compression pipelines, the problem compounds — when you distill an ensemble into a single model, diversity across ensemble members (which provides implicit regularization over attention patterns) is replaced by a single sharpened distribution that has no mechanism to recover the variance it lost. What an expert worries about that a beginner misses is the asymmetry of collapse: perplexity and even BLEU/ROUGE can remain stable or improve slightly through several distillation rounds while entropy collapse is already irreversible, because these metrics don't penalize over-reliance on a narrow attention window until the model is stressed by out-of-distribution inputs or longer contexts. The deeper concern is that confidence sharpening acts as an implicit prior against uncertainty, so any genuine ambiguity in input — which a healthy model should hedge over — gets resolved prematurely and baked into the compressed model's weights with false certainty.
